vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the person who looks after somebody who is ill, often for years and without pay
to make pain or difficulty less severe, without removing it
the shame a society attaches to a condition, which the patient ends up carrying too
the story a patient tells about their own illness, in their own words
the place beside a patient's bed, where the real conversation happens
an account somebody gives of what they lived through, offered so that others hear it
to treat somebody's account as unimportant and not worth listening to
lasting for years, with no expectation of a cure

paras: When a doctor asks what is wrong, the answer arrives as two stories at the same time. One is the story medicine can use: onset, duration, location, intensity. The other is the story the patient actually lives, which begins earlier, includes people who are not in the room, and rarely fits the fifteen minutes available. Narrative medicine, a field that grew out of clinical practice rather than out of literary theory, argues that the second story is not decoration around the first. It is evidence, and a clinician who cannot read it is working with half the record.

The clearest case is chronic illness. A condition that lasts for years does not present a single moment to be diagnosed; it presents a life that has been reorganized around it, and a caregiver whose own days have been reorganized too. Arthur Kleinman, whose work on illness narratives is now read far outside medicine, made the point that the question what is the matter with you produces a list of symptoms, while the question what matters to you produces the account that any treatment will have to work inside. The first question is faster. The second is the one that tells you whether the plan you are about to propose is survivable.

None of this alleviates the pressure clinicians work under, and narrative medicine has been criticized for asking for time that hospitals do not have. Its defenders answer that the alternative is more expensive. A patient whose testimony is dismissed stops offering one, and a silence in the record is not the same as an absence of information. Testimony, in this view, is not a courtesy extended to the suffering. It is a diagnostic instrument, and like any instrument it can be used badly, ignored, or left in the drawer.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: Narrative medicine asks doctors to spend less time with each patient so that more people can be seen.
The story a patient tells is not decoration around the clinical facts: it is evidence, and treating it as evidence changes what a treatment plan can achieve.
Chronic illness cannot be treated at all unless a caregiver is present at every appointment.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: The account she gives is itself evidence.
This is a condition which has no cure, only management.
Kleinman, whose work I keep returning to, puts it differently.
The people who carry most of this are the caregivers.
What matters to you is a different question from what is the matter with you.
A testimony that is dismissed is a testimony that stops being offered.

listenings.text: I trained as a physician and I still think the most useful forty minutes of my week are the ones I spend not treating anybody. I sit with someone who has been ill for a long time and I ask them to tell me how it started, and I do not interrupt. What comes back is almost never a list of symptoms. It is a story about a job that had to be given up, a marriage that reorganized itself around appointments, a mother who moved in. Colleagues tell me that this is lovely but that it is not medicine. My answer is that I have changed treatment plans because of what came out in those forty minutes, and I have never once changed a plan because of a tidier list of symptoms. The story is where the information about adherence lives. If you do not know what a person is protecting, you cannot know what they will and will not do at home.

My wife has been ill for eleven years, so I have been a caregiver for eleven years, and nobody has ever used that word to my face in a hospital. I am the person who remembers the medication schedule, the person who notices the day before a bad week starts, and the person who is standing in the corridor while the conversation that decides everything happens on the other side of a door. What I would say to any clinician listening to this is very simple. Ask me what I have seen. I am not asking to be included out of politeness. I have eleven years of observation that is not in your file, and most of the time nobody has ever asked for it. When somebody finally does ask, it takes ninety seconds and it changes what they decide.
